claims.text: The starting material is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a predominantly FCC, as-built matrix.
Degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases is governed by selective oxidation or reduction of Al and Ti at grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
Grain boundaries and phase interfaces are enriched in Al and Ti.
Al- and Ti-enriched boundaries and interfaces act as preferential sites for oxidation or reduction.
Al and Ti are more reactive than Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni under the proposed exposure conditions.
In air at high temperature, Al and Ti preferentially oxidize.
In hydrogen at high temperature, Al- and Ti-associated regions preferentially undergo reduction and form reduced phases.
The proposed reactions form brittle intergranular oxides or reduced phases.
These intergranular phases embrittle the microstructure and facilitate crack initiation and propagation under stress.
Catastrophic failure occurs when embrittled regions coalesce and cause rapid loss of mechanical integrity.
The controlled intervention is a 50% reduction of both Al and Ti content while keeping the amounts of Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni constant.
Reducing Al and Ti content will decrease formation of brittle intergranular oxides or reduced phases.
The Al/Ti-reduced alloy will have a higher time to failure than the baseline alloy.
The Al/Ti-reduced alloy will retain more ductility and structural integrity than the baseline alloy.
The baseline alloy will exhibit rapid crack propagation and catastrophic failure after exposure.
The proposed governing behavior applies above 600°C for exposure durations up to 100 hours.
Outside the stated temperature and duration range, diffusion and reaction kinetics may differ.
